Part I — GS Paper I — General Studies (Prelims) · Chapter 1: History & Indian Culture

Lesson 1.1.11

Prehistory: Stone Age & Indus Valley Civilisation

In this lessonDetailed StudyRevision DigestKey Points & MindmapDiagrams, Maps & FlowchartsPrevious Year Questions

Detailed Study

The full treatment of this lesson.

MCQ core: match culture → tool type → site → region. Names and pairings below are the tested facts.

1. Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age) — c. 2.6 mya to c. 12,000 BCE

  • Lower: handaxes, cleavers, choppers. Sites: Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu — Acheulian dates pushed back to ~1.5 million years, among the oldest in India), Sohan valley (Pakistan), Bhimbetka (MP), Hunsgi (Karnataka).
  • Middle: flakes, scrapers, borers (Nevasa, Belan valley).
  • Upper: blades, burins, bone tools begin (Bhimbetka paintings begin late phase — hunting, dancing scenes).

2. Mesolithic (c. 10,000–6,000 BCE)

  • Tiny microliths (composite tools); first rock paintings peak (Bhimbetka).
  • Early domestication evidence: Bagor (Rajasthan), Adamgarh (MP) — sheep/goat; Langhnaj (Gujarat).

3. Neolithic (c. 7000–1000 BCE) — first farmers

SiteRegionFirsts / features
MehrgarhBalochistan (Bolan river)Wheat + barley; mud-brick houses; earliest farming in S. Asia (pre-Harappan)
BurzahomKashmirPit-dwellings; stone knives; dog burials
GufkralKashmir'Cave of the potter'; agriculture + tools
ChirandBihar (Ganga)Bone/antler tools industry
Hallur / PiklihalKarnatakaAsh mounds; cattle-keeping
Koldihwa / LahuradewaUP (Belan)Early rice claims (Oryza)

4. Chalcolithic (c. 2800–700 BCE) — copper + stone

  • Cultures: Ahar-Banas (Rajasthan — white-painted black-and-red), Kayatha & Malwa (MP), Jorwe (Maharashtra — Daimabad 'bronze' finds, Inamgaon), Svalda; eastern: Chirand, Pandu Rajar Dhibi.
  • Traits: painted pottery (black-on-red), tiny villages, no bronze tools in bulk — copper scarce; continued stone use.

5. Iron Age & Megalithic (c. 1500–500 BCE south)

  • Megalith burials: South India (Tamil Nadu–Kerala–AP) + Vidarbha (Maharashtra); types: dolmens, cists, menhirs; iron in graves (black-and-red ware).
  • Significance: second urbanisation groundwork — iron plough → surplus → janapadas.

MCQ hooks

  • Mehrgarh = pre-Harappan farming (NOT Harappan town).
  • Burzahom = pit-dwelling (not megalith).
  • Microlith = Mesolithic (not Palaeolithic).
  • Chalcolithic = 'copper-stone'; first to paint pottery in India's villages.
  • Bhimbetka = continuous Palaeolithic→historical rock art (UNESCO).
  • Attirampakkam = Acheulian; Levallois finds (~3.85 lakh BP) rewrote Indian Middle Palaeolithic dates.

6. Reading Prehistory: How We Know What We Know

Prehistory is the one part of the syllabus with no texts. Everything is inferred from three classes of evidence, and UPSC increasingly frames questions around the method rather than the date. Lithic typology classifies stone tools by manufacturing technique — core tools (the nodule itself is shaped) give way to flake tools (the detached piece is the tool), and finally to blade-and-burin industries where a prepared core yields many standardised blanks. This progression is not a calendar; the same technique persists for millennia in some regions while neighbouring valleys have moved on. Stratigraphy reads the vertical sequence of deposits: undisturbed layers place cultures in relative order even without absolute dates. Absolute dating uses radiocarbon (organic material, reliable to ~50,000 years), potassium-argon (volcanic contexts, deep time), and increasingly luminescence dating (OSL/TL), which dates the last time a mineral grain saw sunlight and has been decisive at Attirampakkam.

Why Attirampakkam matters for the exam. Excavations in the Kortallayar basin of Tamil Nadu produced Acheulian handaxes dated by cosmogenic nuclide burial dating to roughly 1.5 million years, and a Middle Palaeolithic (Levallois) assemblage around 385,000 BP. Both results pushed Indian dates far earlier than the textbook consensus and severed the assumption that technological change in India must have arrived with a later migration of modern humans. When a question asks which site "revised the chronology of the Indian Palaeolithic", the answer is Attirampakkam.

7. The Palaeolithic in Depth

The Indian Palaeolithic is conventionally split into three phases, but the boundaries are technological, not chronological, and they overlap heavily across regions.

Lower Palaeolithic — the Acheulian world

The signature artefact is the bifacial handaxe, worked on both faces to a symmetric almond or pear shape, accompanied by cleavers with a straight transverse cutting edge. Raw material dictates form: quartzite dominates peninsular India, producing heavy, robust tools, while the Soan valley of the north-west favoured pebble choppers made on river cobbles — long read as a separate "chopper-chopping tradition", though most archaeologists now treat the difference as raw-material adaptation rather than a distinct culture. Occupation clusters around perennial water and stone sources: the Belan valley (UP), the Narmada basin (where the Hathnora hominin cranium was found), Hunsgi–Baichbal (Karnataka), Didwana (Rajasthan) and Bhimbetka's rock shelters (MP).

Middle Palaeolithic — flakes and prepared cores

Tools shrink and specialise into scrapers, points and borers, struck as flakes from prepared cores. The Levallois technique — shaping a core so that a single predetermined flake of controlled size can be detached — is the diagnostic advance, implying planning several steps ahead. Type sites are Nevasa on the Pravara (which gave the phase its older name, the "Nevasan"), the Belan and Son valleys, and the Luni basin.

Upper Palaeolithic — blades, bone and the first art

Long parallel-sided blades and chisel-like burins appear, along with the first systematic use of bone and antler — the Kurnool caves (Andhra Pradesh) yielded bone tools, and Baghor I in the Son valley produced a triangular stone in a sandstone platform widely interpreted as a shrine, possibly the earliest evidence of ritual in the subcontinent. Ostrich eggshell beads from Patne (Maharashtra), some engraved, confirm both ornament and the former presence of ostrich in India.

8. The Mesolithic Transition

The Mesolithic is defined by the microlith: a blade or bladelet under about five centimetres, often geometric (triangle, trapeze, lunate), designed to be hafted in a row along a wooden or bone shaft with resin. This is composite technology — a broken element is replaced rather than the whole tool discarded — and it underwrites the bow and arrow, harpoons and sickles. It is an economic revolution disguised as a technical one.

The context is climatic. The end of the Pleistocene around 12,000 BP brought warmer, wetter conditions, the retreat of large Ice Age fauna and the spread of smaller, faster game and grasslands. Broad-spectrum foraging replaced big-game hunting. Key sites carry distinct signatures:

SiteRegionWhat it establishes
BagorRajasthan (Kothari river)Largest Mesolithic site in India; earliest evidence of animal domestication (sheep/goat) c. 5000 BCE; long continuity into the Chalcolithic
AdamgarhMadhya PradeshDomesticated cattle, sheep, goat, dog, pig — the widest domesticate range
Sarai Nahar RaiUttar Pradesh (Pratapgarh)Human burials, some with grave goods; evidence of violence (an arrowhead lodged in a rib)
Mahadaha & DamdamaUP (Ganga plain)Large cemeteries; double and triple burials; bone ornaments
LanghnajGujaratMicroliths with wild fauna; contact with Harappan-period pottery in upper levels
BhimbetkaMadhya PradeshDensest rock-art concentration; UNESCO World Heritage Site

Rock art. Bhimbetka's roughly 750 shelters preserve painting from the Upper Palaeolithic through the medieval period — the exam-relevant point is continuity, not antiquity alone. Earliest layers use green and dark red for large animals; Mesolithic layers are the richest, showing hunting parties, dancing, honey collection and communal scenes in linear red; later historic layers add horses, riders and script. Pigments were mineral — haematite for red, limestone for white, manganese for black.

9. The Neolithic: Regional Trajectories, Not One Revolution

V. Gordon Childe's phrase "Neolithic Revolution" implies a single event; India shows at least four largely independent regional developments with different crops, houses and dates. Examiners reward candidates who can name the region-crop-site triad.

  • North-west (Mehrgarh, Balochistan, c. 7000 BCE) — the earliest and most important. A continuous seven-period sequence runs from aceramic farming through pottery, copper and cotton to the threshold of the Harappan cities. Wheat and barley, mud-brick rectangular houses with internal compartments used partly as granaries, burials with turquoise and lapis beads implying long-distance exchange, and a drilled human molar that is the oldest known evidence of dentistry. Mehrgarh proves the Harappan civilisation had deep indigenous roots — a favourite prelims trap where the site is wrongly offered as "a Harappan city".
  • Kashmir (Burzahom, Gufkral, c. 3000–1500 BCE) — the distinctive form is the pit-dwelling, dug into karewa soil, narrow at the top and wide at the base, with steps and post-holes for a roof: an adaptation to cold. Burzahom yields polished stone axes, bone harpoons and needles, coarse grey burnished pottery, and dog burials alongside human graves — a practice not found elsewhere in India. A stone slab engraving shows a hunting scene with what may be a supernova.
  • Eastern India (Chirand, Senuwar, Bihar) — Chirand on the Ganga is famous for an exceptional bone and antler tool industry, plus rice, wheat, barley, lentils and moong.
  • South India (Karnataka–Andhra: Maski, Brahmagiri, Piklihal, Hallur, Sanganakallu, Utnur) — defined by ash mounds, huge accumulations of burnt cattle dung marking seasonal cattle camps, evidencing a pastoral rather than cereal-first Neolithic. Crops were millets, gram and horsegram; the ground stone axe with a pointed butt is the type tool. Hallur is significant for an early iron date, showing the compressed Neolithic-to-Iron transition in the peninsula.
  • North-east (Daojali Hading, Assam) — shouldered celts and cord-impressed pottery, linking the region to a South-East Asian technological sphere rather than a Gangetic one.

The rice question recurs. Koldihwa (UP) produced claims of rice husk in pottery dated as early as 7000 BCE; the dates are contested on contamination grounds. Lahuradewa (Sant Kabir Nagar, UP) provides better-supported evidence of rice around 6400 BCE, making the middle Ganga plain a plausible independent centre of rice domestication. Safe exam answer: Lahuradewa for early rice, with Koldihwa flagged as disputed.

10. Chalcolithic Cultures — the Village Interlude

Chalcolithic ("copper-stone") cultures used copper but had not mastered tin alloying at scale, so stone blades remained in daily use. Crucially, most Indian Chalcolithic cultures are post-Harappan and non-urban: they represent villages, not the rise of cities. Each is identified by its painted pottery.

CultureCore areaDiagnostic pottery & traits
Ahar–BanasSouth-east Rajasthan (Ahar, Balathal, Gilund)White-painted Black-and-Red Ware; abundant copper (local Khetri ore) so few stone blades; Balathal's massive fortification enclosure
KayathaMalwa (MP)Earliest Malwa culture; sturdy chocolate-slipped ware; copper bangles, steatite and agate bead necklaces
MalwaNavdatoli, Eran, NagdaBuff/cream surface with black painting — considered the richest Chalcolithic ceramic; Navdatoli shows the widest crop range
JorweMaharashtra (Inamgaon, Daimabad, Chandoli)Matt-painted black-on-red; Inamgaon's irrigation channel and embankment; five-roomed chief's house; urn burials of children; late-phase decline into pastoralism as rainfall fell
SavaldaTapi valleyEarliest Maharashtra Chalcolithic; weapon-motif pottery
Prabhas & RangpurGujarat (Saurashtra)Late/derived Harappan lustrous red ware

Daimabad deserves separate memory: it yielded four solid bronze objects — a chariot with a driver drawn by two oxen, a rhinoceros, an elephant and a buffalo — the most spectacular Chalcolithic bronzes in India, and it is the southernmost Harappan-affiliated site. Inamgaon is the best-excavated Chalcolithic village and the standard illustration of social differentiation: house size varies, the largest structure sits apart, and burial goods are unequal.

Burial practice is an easy discriminator: in Maharashtra the dead were buried north–south in house floors with the feet chopped off (to prevent the spirit returning, in one reading), while in south India burials were east–west. Children were placed in twin urns joined mouth-to-mouth.

11. The Iron Age and the Megalithic Complex

Iron changes history because iron ore is common while tin is rare — once smelting temperatures are achieved, effective tools cease to be an elite monopoly. Indian evidence for early iron comes from Malhar and Raja Nal-ka-Tila (UP) and Ataranjikhera, with dates pushed back towards 1800–1200 BCE, and from Hallur in the south. The consequence in the Ganga plain was decisive: iron axes cleared dense monsoon forest and the iron-shod plough broke heavy alluvium, generating the agrarian surplus that funded the second urbanisation and the mahajanapadas.

The megalithic tradition of peninsular India (c. 1500–500 BCE, extending into the early historic period) is essentially a burial complex, associated with Black-and-Red Ware and iron grave goods. Learn the typology:

  • Dolmen — a chamber of upright slabs with a capstone, above ground.
  • Cist — a slab-built box grave, usually underground; a port-hole cist has a circular opening cut in one slab.
  • Menhir — a single standing stone, commemorative rather than containing a burial.
  • Cairn circle — a heap of stones ringed by boulders.
  • Umbrella stone (kudakkal) and hood stone (topikal) — mushroom-shaped laterite forms, largely confined to Kerala.
  • Rock-cut cave burials — also a Kerala speciality.

Key sites: Brahmagiri, Maski and Hallur (Karnataka), Adichanallur (Tamil Nadu — urn burials with iron and bronze), Junapani (Nagpur, cairn circles with cup-marks) and the Vidarbha cluster, and Mahurjhari. Many megalithic burials are secondary — the bones were interred after excarnation — and several contain the remains of multiple individuals, suggesting clan or lineage vaults rather than individual graves.

12. Prelims Discrimination Drill

Most prehistory questions are pairing questions. Rehearse the discriminations that examiners actually exploit:

  • Mehrgarh = Neolithic farming, Balochistan, pre-Harappan — not a Harappan city, not in India today.
  • Burzahom = pit-dwellings and dog burials, Kashmir — not megalithic (though menhirs occur late), not Chalcolithic.
  • Microliths = Mesolithic. Handaxes = Lower Palaeolithic. Blades and burins = Upper Palaeolithic. Polished ground axes = Neolithic.
  • Ash mounds = South Indian Neolithic pastoralism (Utnur, Kupgal) — not funerary.
  • Daimabad = Chalcolithic bronzes and southernmost Harappan site.
  • Inamgaon = Jorwe irrigation and social differentiation.
  • Adichanallur = megalithic urn burials, Tamil Nadu.
  • Bhimbetka = rock art, continuous occupation, UNESCO.
  • Chirand = bone-tool industry, Bihar; Lahuradewa = early rice, UP.
  • Chronological order for sequencing questions: Palaeolithic → Mesolithic → Neolithic → Chalcolithic → Iron Age/Megalithic — but remember these overlap regionally, which is itself a favourite statement to judge true or false.

Statement-judging tip. Options that use absolute language — "iron was first used in India at X", "the Neolithic began simultaneously across India", "all megaliths contain human remains" — are almost always false. Indian prehistory is regionally staggered, and the safest instinct is to reject uniformity claims.

Revision Digest

Condensed for the last mile before the exam.

Prelims GS-I › History & Culture › Ancient History. Site–feature matching (especially Harappan) recurs almost every year.

Stone Age ladder

  • Palaeolithic (up to ~10,000 BCE): Lower — Soan valley (pebble tools), Bhimbetka, Attirampakkam, Hunsgi; Middle — Nevasa, Bhimbetka (flakes); Upper — Bhimbetka paintings, Patne, bone tools at Kurnool caves; Homo erectus Hathnora (Narmada) skull.
  • Mesolithic (~10,000–6,000 BCE): microliths; Bagor (Rajasthan; earliest domestication evidence claim), Adamgarh (MP), Langhnaj (Gujarat), Sarai Nahar Rai & Mahadaha (UP; burials), Bhimbetka rock art.
  • Neolithic: Mehrgarh (Balochistan; c. 7000 BCE; wheat-barley, cattle; pre-Harappan), Burzahom (Kashmir; pit dwellings, dog burials), Gufkral, Chirand (Bihar; bone tools), Koldihwa (rice claim ~6000 BCE), Hallur, Maski, Piklihal, Sanganakallu, Utnur (ash mounds — South), Daojali Hading (Assam).
  • Chalcolithic cultures: Ahar-Banas (Rajasthan; copper, Gilund), Kayatha, Malwa (Navdatoli), Jorwe (Inamgaon, Daimabad — largest; bronze rhinoceros/chariot hoard), Savalda, OCP/Copper Hoards (Ganga-Yamuna; anthropomorphs), Ganeshwar (copper source for Harappans?).

Harappan/Indus (c. 2600–1900 BCE mature)

  • Phases: Early (3300–2600; Kot Diji, Amri, Sothi), Mature (2600–1900), Late (1900–1300; Cemetery H, Jhukar, Rangpur, Lustrous Red Ware).
  • Discovery: Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni 1921), Mohenjo-daro (R.D. Banerji 1922); John Marshall announced 1924; largest sites: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi (largest in India), Dholavira.
SiteRiver/StateSignature finding
HarappaRavi, Punjab (Pak)granaries, coffin burial, red-sandstone torso, workmen's quarters
Mohenjo-daroIndus, SindhGreat Bath, Great Granary, bronze dancing girl, Pashupati seal, priest-king, assembly hall
ChanhudaroIndus, Sindhonly city without citadel; bead factory, ink pot
LothalBhogava, Gujaratdockyard, rice husk, fire altars, double burial, ivory scale
KalibanganGhaggar, Rajasthanploughed field, fire altars, wooden drains, camel bones, earthquake evidence
DholaviraKadir island, Gujaratthree-tier city, water reservoirs, signboard, stadium; UNESCO 2021
RakhigarhiHisar, Haryanalargest Indian site; DNA study (2019)
BanawaliHaryanabarley, oval settlement, terracotta plough
SurkotadaGujarathorse bones (disputed)
DaimabadMaharashtrasouthernmost
MandaJammunorthernmost
AlamgirpurUPeasternmost
SutkagendorBalochistanwesternmost; trade post
RoparPunjabdog buried with human
Balakot / Kot Diji / AmriPakearly Harappan
ShortughaiAfghanistanlapis lazuli outpost
  • Features: grid planning, baked bricks 1:2:4, drainage, standard weights (binary/decimal; 16 base), seals (steatite; unicorn commonest), undeciphered script — boustrophedon, no temples/palaces unambiguously, cotton earliest, copper-bronze (no iron), wheel-made pottery (red-black), trade with Mesopotamia (Meluhha; Dilmun = Bahrain, Magan = Oman), Mother goddess, Pashupati, peepal, bull worship, no horse (contested).
  • Decline theories: Aryan invasion (Wheeler; discredited), floods (Marshall, Dales), tectonic/river shift (Raikes; Ghaggar-Hakra drying), ecological (Fairservis), climate change/monsoon weakening.

Traps

  • Ploughed field = Kalibangan; dockyard = Lothal; Great Bath = Mohenjo-daro; citadel-less = Chanhudaro.
  • Harappans knew bronze, not iron; script is undeciphered; Rakhigarhi (not Dholavira) is the largest in India by area.

Key Points & Mindmap

Skeleton facts and recall triggers.

Rapid-fire pairs. Cover the right column, recall the left.

Site flash

  • Attirampakkam — Acheulian, oldest Indian handaxe culture (TN).
  • Bhimbetka — rock shelters, paintings (MP).
  • Bagor / Adamgarh — earliest animal domestication (Raj/MP).
  • Mehrgarh — wheat-barley farming, pre-Harappan (Balochistan).
  • Burzahom — pit-dwellings, dog burials (Kashmir).
  • Chirand — bone tools (Bihar).
  • Hallur — ash mounds, cattle (Karnataka).
  • Daimabad — bronze chariot/rhinoceros finds (Jorwe, MH).
  • Inamgaon — Jorwe village, granary (MH).
  • Brahmagiri — megaliths + ash mounds (Karnataka).

Culture flash

  • Palaeolithic → handaxes → Mesolithic → microliths → Neolithic → farming, pottery → Chalcolithic → copper + painted ware → Iron/Megalith → burials, plough.
  • Black-and-red ware = Chalcolithic & Megalith signature.
  • First rice: Koldihwa/Lahuradewa (UP); first wheat-barley: Mehrgarh.

Confusables

  • Mehrgarh ≠ Harappa (pre-Harappan, different river — Bolan vs Ravi).
  • Megalith = burial monument ≠ megalithic = iron culture label.
  • Burzahom pit-house ≠ Chalcolithic mud-house.
  • Bronze Age label: applied to Harappan (urban bronze), not to village Chalcolithic cultures.

Part I — GS Paper I — General Studies (Prelims) · Chapter 1: History & Indian Culture

Lesson 1.1.12

Vedic Age & Later Vedic Period

In this lessonDetailed StudyRevision DigestKey Points & MindmapDiagrams, Maps & FlowchartsPrevious Year Questions

Detailed Study

The full treatment of this lesson.

Two Vedic ages, one text ladder. UPSC tests text→content, god→period, term→meaning.

1. Early Vedic / Rigvedic (c. 1500–1000 BCE)

  • Homeland: Sapta-Sindhu (Indus + Saraswati belt). Rigveda's oldest mandalas = II–VII (family books); X (Purusha sukta — varna origin).
  • Economy: pastoral — cow = wealth unit (go-dhana); godhuli = distance; agriculture minor; nishka = gold ornament (later coin-name).
  • Polity: tribe (jana) based; raja = war-leader elected-ish; sabha & samiti check king; officers: senani, gramani, purohita; bali voluntary tribute (no regular tax yet).
  • Society: dasa varna (early class colour), women visible (Lopamudra, Ghosha, Apala; no child marriage, widow could remarry).
  • Religion: personified nature — Indra (~250 hymns, war/rain), Varuna (rita), Agni (messenger), Soma; worship = hymn + sacrifice, no temples/idols.

2. Later Vedic (c. 1000–600 BCE)

  • Texts: Yajur, Sama, Atharva + Brahmanas + Aranyakas + early Upanishads; geography pushes east ( Videha, Kuru-Panchala).
  • Economy: iron (shyama ayas / krishna ayas) → plough, rice-wheat; occupations hereditary; nishka/satamana as value units.
  • Polity: janapadas; hereditary kingship; grand rites — rajasuya (consecration), vajapeya (chariot race), ashvamedha (imperial claim); sabha declines to elite council.
  • Society: varna hardens (Brahmana–Kshatriya–Vaishya–Shudra); 4 ashramas codified (Jabala Upanishad); women's status drops (no early-Vedic participation).
  • Religion: Prajapati (creator) tops; Rudra, Vishnu rise; sacrifice becomes mechanical (Brahmana literature = rule-books).
  • Reaction: Upanishads (c. 800–500 BCE) — atmabrahma monism (Yajnavalkya–Maitreyi dialogues).

3. The text ladder (memorise order + pairs)

LayerContentExample
SamhitasHymns (4 Vedas)Rigveda — 1028 hymns, 10 mandalas
BrahmanasRitual proseAitareya (Rig), Satapatha (Yajur)
AranyakasForest meditationsBridge to Upanishads
UpanishadsPhilosophy108 total; 11 principal; Chandogya, Brihadaranyaka
Vedangas (6)Limbs for Veda studyShiksha, Kalpa, Vyakarana, Nirukta, Chhanda, Jyotisha

MCQ hooks

  • Gayatri mantra = RV 3.62.10 (the Savitri; composed in the gayatri meter).
  • 'Ayas' = metal generally in RV; iron specifically appears later Vedic.
  • Upaveda pairs: Ayurveda–Rig, Dhanurveda–Yajur, Gandharvaveda–Sama, Shilpaveda–Atharva.
  • Purusha sukta (RV X) = first varna statement; Vaishya term appears first here.
  • Atharvaveda = folk beliefs, medicine, magic — 'Veda of magical formulae'.
  • Uttaramerur ≠ Vedic (that's Chola); Vedic assemblies = sabha/samiti/vidatha/gana.

Revision Digest

Condensed for the last mile before the exam.

Prelims GS-I › History & Culture › Ancient History. Text-classification and social-term questions dominate.

Sources & chronology

  • Early/Rig Vedic c. 1500–1000 BCE (Sapta Sindhu — Punjab, Afghanistan); Later Vedic c. 1000–600 BCE (Ganga-Yamuna doab; Kuru-Panchala); archaeology: Painted Grey Ware (PGW) = later Vedic; iron (shyama/krishna ayas) from ~1000 BCE (Atranjikhera).
  • Boghaz-Koi (Hittite–Mitanni) inscription 1400 BCE — Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Nasatya.

The four Vedas

VedaContentBrahmanaUpanishad (main)Hook
Rig1,028 hymns, 10 mandalas (2–7 family books oldest; 10th latest — Purusha Sukta, Nasadiya)Aitareya, KaushitakiAitareya, KaushitakiGayatri mantra (3rd mandala, Vishvamitra, to Savitri); hotri priest
Samamelodies (1,549 verses; 75 original)Panchavimsha, JaiminiyaChandogya, Kenaudgatri; origin of Indian music
Yajursacrificial formulae; Shukla (Vajasaneyi) & Krishna (Taittiriya)Shatapatha (Shukla), TaittiriyaBrihadaranyaka, Isha (Shukla); Taittiriya, Katha, Shvetashvatara (Krishna)adhvaryu
Atharvacharms, medicine, popular beliefsGopathaMundaka, Mandukya, Prashnabrahman priest; latest; not trayi
  • Vedangas (6): Shiksha (phonetics), Kalpa (ritual; Shrauta/Grihya/Dharma/Shulba sutras), Vyakarana (grammar — Panini Ashtadhyayi), Nirukta (etymology — Yaska), Chhanda (metre), Jyotisha (astronomy).
  • Upavedas: Ayurveda (Rig), Gandharvaveda (Sama), Dhanurveda (Yajur), Shilpa/Arthaveda (Atharva).
  • Six darshanas (later): Samkhya (Kapila), Yoga (Patanjali), Nyaya (Gautama), Vaisheshika (Kanada), Mimamsa (Jaimini), Vedanta (Badarayana).

Rig Vedic society & polity

  • Tribal (jana), rajan not hereditary rigidly; assemblies sabha, samiti, vidatha, gana; purohita (Vasishtha, Vishvamitra), senani; bali voluntary; Dasarajna — Battle of Ten Kings (Sudas of Bharatas on the Parushni/Ravi).
  • Pastoral: cow = wealth (gavishti = war), gomat; barley (yava); horse chariot; rivers: Sindhu, Vitasta (Jhelum), Asikni (Chenab), Parushni (Ravi), Vipas (Beas), Shutudri (Sutlej), Sarasvati (most sacred), Drishadvati, Kubha (Kabul), Gomati (Gomal); Ganga once, Yamuna thrice.
  • Gods: Indra (250 hymns; Purandara), Agni (200), Varuna (rita), Soma, Surya, Savitri, Pushan, Ushas, Aditi (goddesses minor); no temples/idols.
  • Women: Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra, Vishvavara — hymn composers; sabha attendance; no child marriage; widow remarriage/niyoga.
  • Varna: Purusha Sukta (10th mandala) — first mention of four varnas.

Later Vedic changes

  • Territorial kingdoms (rashtra; janapada), hereditary kingship, grand sacrifices rajasuya, vajapeya, ashvamedha; titles samrat, ekrat; ratnins (12 jewels); sabha-samiti decline, vidatha disappears; bali compulsory, bhaga, shulka.
  • Agriculture central (rice vrihi, wheat godhuma); varna rigid; gotra appears; four ashramas (Jabala Upanishad first); women's status falls (Aitareya — daughter a misery; but Gargi & Maitreyi in Brihadaranyaka); Shatapatha Brahmana — Videgha Mathava's eastward move; Prajapati, Vishnu, Rudra rise; Pushan becomes Shudra god.
  • Upanishads (108 traditional; 13 principal) — atman-brahman, karma, moksha; tat tvam asi (Chandogya), aham brahmasmi (Brihadaranyaka), Satyameva Jayate (Mundaka).

Traps

  • Gayatri is in the Rig (3rd mandala), addressed to Savitri; Nasadiya & Purusha Sukta in the 10th.
  • Atharva is outside the trayi; Shatapatha is a Yajur Brahmana; Chandogya is Sama.
  • Iron appears in the later Vedic age (PGW), not Rig Vedic (which had copper/bronze — ayas).

Skeleton facts and recall triggers.

Fact pairs for last-hour revision.

Pairs flash

  • Oldest Veda → Rigveda · family mandalas → II–VII · latest → X (Purusha sukta).
  • Iron → shyama ayas · plough → sira/ langala · god-of-rain-early → Indra.
  • Sacrifices → rajasuya (coronation), vajapeya (race), ashvamedha (empire).
  • Tax early → bali (voluntary) · officer → senani/gramani/purohita.
  • Brahmana pairs → Aitareya-Rig · Satapatha-Yajur · Tandya/Panchavimsha-Sama · Gopatha-Atharva.
  • Upanishad count → 108 (Muktika); principal → 11-13; Brihadaranyaka = largest.
  • Women RV seers → Lopamudra, Ghosha, Apala, Vishwavara.
  • Upaveda → Ayur/Dhanur/Gandharva/Shilpa × Rig/Yajur/Sama/Atharva.
  • Soma = plant juice oblation · Yajna = fire ritual · Rita = cosmic order (Varuna).
  • Kuru-Panchala = Later-Vedic heartland (Brahmana literature zone).

Early → Later shift (6 keywords)

  • Pastoral → agrarian-iron · tribe → janapada · elected-ish → hereditary · sabha strong → elite · fluid varna → rigid · nature-gods → Prajapati-ritualism.

Trap flash

  • No temples/idols in Vedic worship (idol-yajna = later Puranic).
  • 'Dasa varna' ≠ caste system yet (Arya vs Dasa, colour-based).
  • Ashrama-4 codified in Upanishad era, not Rigvedic.
  • Sita (furrow) term later; Vedic taxes = bali (offering), bhaga (king's share).

Part I — GS Paper I — General Studies (Prelims) · Chapter 1: History & Indian Culture

Lesson 1.1.13

Mahajanapadas, Buddhism, Jainism & Mauryan Empire

In this lessonDetailed StudyRevision DigestKey Points & MindmapDiagrams, Maps & FlowchartsPrevious Year Questions

Detailed Study

The full treatment of this lesson.

The making of the first empire: 16 states → Magadha → Nandas → Maurya → Ashoka's dhamma. UPSC loves ruler→measure and edict→place pairs.

1. The 16 Mahajanapadas (6th c. BCE)

  • Source: Anguttara Nikaya (Buddhist) + Bhagavati Sutra (Jain list varies). Monarchies (Magadha, Kosala, Kashi, Vatsa...) vs ganasanghas/republics (Vajji — Licchavis of Vaishali, Malla, Shakyas of Kapilavastu).
  • Why Magadha wins: iron ore (Jharkhand belts), fertile Ganga valley, elephants, riverine trade, ambitious rulers, capitals Rajagriha → Pataliputra (Udayin — confluence point).

2. Magadhan rise

DynastyKey rulersNotes
HaryankaBimbisara (contemporary of Buddha/Mahavira — matrimony with Kosala/Lichchavi), Ajatashatru (Vaisali war; war-engines mahashilakantaka, rathamushala), Udayin (founds Pataliputra)c. 544–412 BCE
ShishunagaShishunaga (destroys Avanti power), Kalashoka (2nd Buddhist Council, Vaishali 383 BCE)c. 412–345
NandaMahapadma ('second Parashurama', destroyer of Kshatriyas), Dhana Nanda (Alexander's era; unpopular taxation)c. 345–322

3. Alexander (326 BCE)

  • Crossed Indus 326; Hydaspes (Jhelum) battle vs Porus (Puru) — impressed, restored him; army mutinied at Beas (Hyphasis); retreat via Makran; died 323 Babylon. Effects: trade routes, Greek colonies, Seleucus successor.

4. Mauryan Empire (c. 322–185 BCE)

  • Chandragupta (with Kautilya — Arthashastra): 305 Seleucus pact — marriage alliance, Arachosia/Kandahar ceded, Megasthenes ambassador (Indica). Jain tradition: became Bhadrabahu follower, died at Shravanabelagola.
  • Bindusara: 'Amitraghata'; Deccan up to Mysore (except Kalinga); Ajivika leanings.
  • Ashoka (268–232): Kalinga 261 (13th Rock Edict — remorse, dhamma-vijaya instead of bheri-ghosha); officials: dhamma mahamattas (14th year); tours; edicts in Prakrit (Brahmi script — most; Kharoshthi NW: Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra; bilingual Greek-Aramaic: Kandahar); 14 Major Rock Edicts (Kalsi, Girnar, Dhauli, Jaugada...), 7 Pillar Edicts (Delhi-Topra, Delhi-Meerut, Lauriya-Araraj...); Sarnath lion capital = national emblem; chakra = flag wheel.
  • Administration: saptanga (7 limbs), 18 tirthas (mantrin top), provinces at Ujjain, Taxila, Tosali, Suvarnagiri (+Pataliputra); army per Megasthenes (6,00,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry, 9,000 elephants); revenue: bhaga = 1/6, sita lands, punch-marked silver panas (karshapana family); espionage (gudhapurusha), urban officials (nagaraka, 30-member? committees per Arthashastra).
  • Art: monolithic polished pillars, stupas (Sanchi core), Barabar caves (Lomas Rishi — first), Yaksha-Yakshini sculpture (Didarganj).
  • Decline: 185 Pushyamitra (Brahmanical reaction + economic-fiscal + succession readings).

MCQ hooks

  • 2nd Buddhist Council = Vaishali, Kalashoka's time (1st = Rajgriha, Ajatashatru).
  • Kharoshthi edicts = only Shahbazgarhi & Mansehra; rest Brahmi.
  • Bilingual (Greek-Aramaic) = Kandahar only.
  • Tosali = eastern province (Kalinga); Suvarnagiri = southern.
  • 'Devanam Piya' = beloved of gods (Ashoka's title; named only in Maski, Gujarra, Nettur, Udegolam — Minor REs).
  • Megasthenes = Indica (fragments via Strabo/Arrian); Deimachos (Bindusara, Antiochus I), Dionysius (Ashoka, sent to Ptolemy II of Egypt).

Revision Digest

Condensed for the last mile before the exam.

Prelims GS-I › History & Culture › Ancient History. Heaviest-weighted ancient block: religion facts + Ashokan edicts + Mauryan administration.

Sixteen Mahajanapadas (c. 6th BCE; Anguttara Nikaya, Bhagavati Sutra)

  • Monarchies: Magadha (Rajgir/Girivraja → Pataliputra), Kosala (Shravasti; Prasenajit), Vatsa (Kaushambi; Udayana), Avanti (Ujjain/Mahishmati; Pradyota), Anga (Champa), Kashi (Varanasi), Chedi (Shuktimati), Matsya (Viratnagar), Shurasena (Mathura), Ashmaka (Potali/Paudanya — only one south of Vindhyas, Godavari), Gandhara (Taxila), Kamboja (Rajpur/Hatak).
  • Republics (gana-sanghas): Vajji/Vrijji (Vaishali; Licchavis), Malla (Kusinara & Pava), Kuru (Indraprastha), Panchala (Ahichchhatra & Kampilya).
  • Magadha's rise: Haryanka (Bimbisara — Gandhaka army, matrimonial; Ajatashatru — war engines rathamusala, mahashilakantaka; Vaishali conquest; Udayin founded Pataliputra) → Shishunaga (Avanti annexed; Vaishali capital) → Nandas (Mahapadma — ekarat, sarvakshatrantaka; Dhana Nanda vs Alexander's time) → Mauryas.
  • Persian: Cyrus, Darius I 516 BCE (Gandhara 20th satrapy; Kharosthi script origin). Alexander 326 BCE — Hydaspes (Jhelum) vs Porus; returned from Beas; died Babylon 323.

Buddhism

  • Siddhartha b. Lumbini 563 BCE (Shakya; Suddhodana, Mahamaya; Gautami); Mahabhinishkramana 29; enlightenment Bodh Gaya (Uruvela) at 35; first sermon Sarnath — Dhammachakrapravartana (Panchavargiya); Mahaparinirvana Kusinara 483 BCE (Malla); symbols: lotus/bull (birth), horse (renunciation), bodhi tree, wheel, stupa.
  • Doctrine: Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path (Ashtangika marga), Middle Path, Pratityasamutpada, anatta, anicca, dukkha; Three Jewels; Nirvana; no soul/god.
  • Councils: I Rajgir 483 (Mahakassapa; Ajatashatru; Vinaya-Upali, Sutta-Ananda) · II Vaishali 383 (Sabakami; Kalashoka; Sthaviravadins vs Mahasanghikas) · III Pataliputra 250 (Moggaliputta Tissa; Ashoka; Abhidhamma; Kathavatthu) · IV Kundalvana, Kashmir 1st c. CE (Vasumitra/Ashvaghosha; Kanishka; Hinayana–Mahayana split; Mahavibhasha).
  • Texts: Tripitaka (Pali) — Vinaya, Sutta (5 Nikayas incl. Jataka in Khuddaka), Abhidhamma; Milindapanho (Nagasena–Menander); Buddhacharita (Ashvaghosha); Mahayana — Nagarjuna (Madhyamika, shunyata), Asanga–Vasubandhu (Yogachara); Vajrayana (Tantric; Bihar-Bengal, Palas). Women admitted at Vaishali (Gautami; Ananda's plea).

Jainism

  • 24 Tirthankaras; Rishabhanatha (bull) first; Parshvanatha (23rd; 4 vows; snake; Varanasi); Mahavira (24th; b. Kundagrama/Vaishali 540 BCE; Siddhartha & Trishala (Licchavi); kaivalya at Jrimbhikagrama, river Rijupalika, sal tree, age 42; Jina/Nirgrantha; died Pavapuri 468 BCE, age 72; lion symbol).
  • Five vows (Mahavira added brahmacharya); triratna — right faith, knowledge, conduct; anekantavada/syadvada (sapta-bhangi); jiva in everything; extreme ahimsa; sallekhana; no creator god, but souls & gods exist.
  • Councils: I Pataliputra c. 300 BCE (Sthulabhadra; 12 Angas compiled; Bhadrabahu to south with Chandragupta → Shvetambara–Digambara split) · II Vallabhi 512 CE (Devardhi Kshamashramana; final canon in Ardha-Magadhi Prakrit).
  • Patrons: Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, Chandragupta Maurya, Kharavela (Hathigumpha; Kalinga Jina), Chalukya Kumarapala, Amoghavarsha; Shravanabelagola (Gomateshwara/Bahubali 983 CE, Ganga minister Chamundaraya).

Mauryan Empire (321–185 BCE)

  • Chandragupta (321–297): Nanda overthrow (Chanakya/Kautilya Arthashastra, Vishakhadatta Mudrarakshasa), Seleucus 305 (Herat, Kandahar, Kabul, Makran; 500 elephants; Megasthenes Indica), Jain, died Shravanabelagola. Bindusara (Amitraghata; Deimachus; Ajivika). Ashoka (268/273–232): Kalinga 261 BCE (8th year), Dhamma, Dhamma-mahamattas (14th year), missions (Mahinda & Sanghamitta to Sri Lanka — Tissa; Yavana kings named in RE XIII: Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas, Alexander), Devanampiya Piyadasi; name "Ashoka" in Maski, Gujarra, Nittur, Udegolam minor rock edicts.
  • Edicts: 14 Major Rock Edicts (Girnar, Kalsi, Shahbazgarhi & Mansehra (Kharosthi), Dhauli & Jaugada (separate Kalinga edicts; no RE XI–XIII), Sopara, Yerragudi, Sannati); 7 Pillar Edicts (Topra/Delhi has all 7; Lauriya-Nandangarh, Lauriya-Araraj, Rampurva, Allahabad/Kaushambi (Queen's edict; Schism), Sanchi, Sarnath); Bhabru/Bairat (Buddhist texts); Lumbini/Rummindei (tax reduced to 1/8; bali exempt); Nigali Sagar (Konakamana stupa); Kandahar bilingual Greek–Aramaic; Lampaka Aramaic. Brahmi deciphered James Prinsep 1837.
  • Administration (Arthashastra + Megasthenes): Saptanga state; Mantriparishad; tirthas (18 high officials); provinces (Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali, Suvarnagiri; kumaras); samaharta (revenue), sannidhata (treasury), rajukas (rural justice, Ashoka), yuktas, pradeshikas; espionage (sanstha, sanchara); Megasthenes' 30-member city council (6 boards of 5); 7 castes (Megasthenes; erroneous); sita (crown land), bhaga 1/6.
  • Art: Sarnath lion capital (national emblem), Rampurva bull, Sankisa elephant, Vaishali single lion; polished Chunar sandstone; Barabar & Nagarjuni caves (Lomas Rishi; Ajivikas); Sanchi stupa core; Didarganj Yakshi (Mauryan polish); Dhauli rock elephant; woodwork palace (Kumrahar 80-pillared hall).
  • Decline 185 BCE: Pushyamitra Shunga killed Brihadratha; theories — brahmanical reaction (Haraprasad Sastri), financial crisis (D.D. Kosambi), pacifism (H.C. Raychaudhuri), weak successors, centralised structure (Romila Thapar).

Traps

  • Mahavira died at Pavapuri, Buddha at Kusinara; both were Kshatriya princes.
  • Third Buddhist council = Ashoka; fourth = Kanishka; Jain Vallabhi council = 512 CE.
  • Kalinga war in the 8th regnal year; Ashoka's personal name appears in Maski-type minor edicts, not the major ones.

Key Points & Mindmap

Skeleton facts and recall triggers.

Pair-recall sheet.

Pairs flash

  • 16 list source → Anguttara Nikaya · republics → Vajji, Malla, Shakya.
  • Pataliputra founder → Udayin · siege machines → Ajatashatru.
  • 2nd Council → Vaishali, Kalashoka · Nanda epithet → 'second Parashurama' (Mahapadma).
  • Alexander's battle → Hydaspes/Jhelum × Porus · turn-back → Beas.
  • Arthashastra → Kautilya · Indica → Megasthenes · Seleucus treaty → 305 BCE.
  • Kalinga war → 261 BCE, 13th RE · dhamma officials → mahamattas.
  • Provinces → Ujjain, Taxila, Tosali, Suvarnagiri · script NW → Kharoshthi.
  • Named Ashoka edicts → Maski, Gujarra, Nettur, Udegolam · bilingual → Kandahar.
  • Lion capital → Sarnath · first caves → Barabar (Lomas Rishi) · Didarganj → Yakshini.
  • Tax → bhaga 1/6 · coin → karshapana/pana · spy → gudhapurusha · city head → nagaraka.

Order flash

  • Haryanka → Shishunaga → Nanda → Maurya (dynasties of Magadha).
  • Maurya line: Chandragupta → Bindusara → Ashoka → (Dasaratha, Samprati...) → Brihadratha (killed by Pushyamitra Sunga, 185 BCE).

Trap flash

  • Ashoka in Buddhist texts only (Divyavadana, Ashokavadana, Mahavamsa) — name absent from his own major edicts.
  • Kalinga = 13th RE content, but Kalinga edicts = separate Dhauli/Jaugada RE set (RE 11-13 replaced).
  • Sanchi stupa core = Ashoka; railing/doors later (Sungas/Satavahanas).
  • Punch-marked coins pre-Mauryan (janapadas) — not invented by Mauryas.

Part I — GS Paper I — General Studies (Prelims) · Chapter 1: History & Indian Culture

Lesson 1.1.14

Post-Mauryan & Gupta Empire

In this lessonDetailed StudyRevision DigestKey Points & MindmapDiagrams, Maps & FlowchartsPrevious Year Questions

Detailed Study

The full treatment of this lesson.

Successor states (185 BCE–320 CE) → the 'classical' Guptas (320–550) → Harsha (606–647). Tests: ruler→book/inscription, era→founder, art→school.

1. Successor states (185 BCE – 320 CE)

PowerKey facts
Sungas (185–73)Pushyamitra kills Brihadratha; Pataliputra/Vidisha; horse sacrifice revival; Sanchi stupa-2 railing; Patanjali (Mahabhashya) tradition
Indo-GreeksFirst coins with king-portraits in India; Menander (Milinda) — dialogue with Nagasena = Milindapanha; Heliodorus pillar (Besnagar — Bhagavata worship proof)
Shakas5 branches; Western Kshatrapas long-lived; Rudradaman I — Junagadh inscription (first major chaste-Sanskrit record; Sudarshana lake repaired, originally Mauryan); Vikram Samvat 57 BCE = victory over Shakas legend
Parthians (Pahlavas)Gondophernes — St. Thomas mission tradition
Kushanas (1st–3rd CE)Kujula → Vima → Kanishka (78 CE — Saka era start); capitals Purushpura (Peshawar) + Mathura; empire on Silk Road; 4th Buddhist Council (Kashmir, Vasumitra chair, Ashvaghosha vice — Mahayana boost); Gandhara + Mathura art (Buddha image appears); Kanishka's stupa at Peshawar
Satavahanas (Deccan)Simuka → Gautamiputra Satakarni (Nasik inscription by mother Gautami Balashri); Prakrit court; lead coins (potin too); first land-grants to brahmanas/buddhists; Amaravati & Nagarjunakonda stupas; guilds (nasik cave record)
Sangam SouthPandyas (Madurai, pearls), Cheras (Kerala, Muziris spice port — Roman coins), Cholas (Uraiyur/Puhar — Kaveripoompattinam); Roman trade: Yavana warehouses, pepper export; Tolkappiyam grammar

2. Gupta age (320–550)

  • Line: Chandragupta I (320 — Gupta era; Lichchhavi marriage) → Samudragupta (Prayaga Prashasti/Allahabad Pillar by court-poet Harisena; aryavarta-dakshinapatha policy; ashvamedha type) → Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' (Ujjain; Fa-Hien visits 399-414; Navaratna incl. Kalidasa; silver coins; Shakas of Gujarat end) → Kumaragupta I (Nalanda founded; Mahendraditya title) → Skandagupta (Hun wars; Sudarshana again; Bhitari pillar).
  • Administration: less centralised than Maurya; land grants (agrahara) with fiscal-immunity → feudal seeds; officers: kumaramatya, sandhivigrahika, mahadandanayaka.
  • Golden-age inventory: Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya 499 — zero-place value, pi, eclipses), Varahamihira (Brihatsamhita), Dhanvantari-Sushruta lineage (medicine), Kalidasa (Abhijnana Shakuntalam), Vishnu Sharma (Panchatantra?), metallurgy: Mehrauli iron pillar (Chandra — rust-free), gold dinar coins; art: Ajanta murals (XVI, XVII), Dashavatara Deogarh (first panchayatana brick temple), Sarn Buddha (Sarnath); universities: Nalanda (Kumaragupta I), Valabhi.
  • Decline: Hunas (Toramana, Mihirakula), land-fragmentation, trade dip; Magadha passes to Maukharis → Harsha (Thanesar + Kannauj; Harshacharita by Banabhatta; Xuanzang visits Nalanda; Kannauj & Prayag assemblies; Ratnavali authorship; after 647 — tripartite war begins).

MCQ hooks

  • Saka era = Kanishka 78 CE; Vikram Samvat = 57 BCE; Gupta era = 320 CE.
  • First Sanskrit-inscription fame = Rudradaman (Junagadh).
  • Kanishka's council city = Kundalvana, Kashmir.
  • Fa-Hien (Gupta-II) vs Xuanzang (Harsha) vs I-tsing (later, 7th-end).
  • Prayaga Prashasti = Harisena; Aihole inscription = Ravikirti (Pulakesin II — coming in medieval list).
  • Mehrauli pillar king 'Chandra' usually read as Chandragupta II.

Revision Digest

Condensed for the last mile before the exam.

Prelims GS-I › History & Culture › Ancient History. Dynasty–ruler–inscription/coin–art school matching, plus Gupta "golden age" facts.

Post-Mauryan dynasties

  • Shungas (185–73 BCE; Pushyamitra — ashvamedha; Patanjali Mahabhashya; Bharhut stupa railings, Sanchi gateways began; Heliodorus pillar Besnagar 113 BCE — Garuda pillar, Bhagavata; Agnimitra — Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram) → Kanvas (Vasudeva 73 BCE).
  • Satavahanas (Deccan; Simuka; Pratishthana/Paithan & Amaravati; Gautamiputra Satakarni — Nasik prashasti by Gautami Balashri; destroyed Shakas (Nahapana coins restruck); Vasishthiputra Pulumavi; Yajna Sri Satakarni — ship coins; lead coins; Prakrit; matronymics; land grants to Brahmanas (earliest — Naneghat, Naganika); Karle, Bhaja, Kanheri chaitya; Amaravati school, Nagarjunakonda; Gathasaptasati (Hala); Brihatkatha (Gunadhya, Paishachi)).
  • Indo-Greeks (Demetrius, Menander/Milinda — Sakala/Sialkot; Nagasena; first gold coins in India; portrait coins; Gandhara art influence; Heliodorus).
  • Shakas (Maues; Western Kshatrapas — Rudradaman I — Junagadh inscription 150 CE, first long Sanskrit inscription; Sudarshana lake repair (built by Pushyagupta under Chandragupta Maurya, conduits by Tushaspa under Ashoka); Vikram Samvat 58 BCE (Vikramaditya of Ujjain legend); Shaka Samvat 78 CE = Kanishka).
  • Parthians/Pahlavas (Gondophernes; St Thomas tradition 1st c. CE).
  • Kushanas (Yuezhi; Kujula Kadphises; Vima Kadphises — gold coins, Shiva; Kanishka 78 CE — Purushapura/Peshawar; Mathura second capital; fourth Buddhist council; Ashvaghosha, Vasumitra, Charaka (Charaka Samhita), Nagarjuna; Mathura & Gandhara schools; headless statue at Mat; Rabatak inscription; Silk Road; Roman trade — Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, Arikamedu; largest number of copper coins).
  • Kharavela of Kalinga (Chedi/Mahameghavahana; Hathigumpha inscription, Udayagiri; Jain; 1st c. BCE).
  • Sangam South: Cheras (Vanji; Senguttuvan — Pattini cult), Cholas (Uraiyur/Puhar; Karikala — Kallanai/Grand Anicut, Venni), Pandyas (Madurai; Sangam patrons; Nedunjeliyan); Tolkappiyam, Ettutogai, Pattuppattu, Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal), Manimekalai (Sattanar); tinai landscapes; Muvendar; vellalar; Yavana trade at Muziris.

Art schools

SchoolPatronMaterialTraits
GandharaKushanagrey schist, stuccoGreco-Roman, wavy hair, drapery, Bamiyan
MathuraKushanared spotted sandstoneindigenous, Yaksha tradition, Jain & Hindu images too, halo
AmaravatiSatavahana/Ikshvakuwhite marblenarrative panels, tribhanga, Nagarjunakonda

Guptas (c. 320–550 CE)

  • Sri Gupta → Ghatotkacha → Chandragupta I (320 CE; Maharajadhiraja; Licchavi marriage — Kumaradevi coins) → Samudragupta (c. 335–75; Allahabad/Prayag prashasti by Harishena on Ashokan pillar — 12 Dakshinapatha kings defeated & restored, 9 Aryavarta uprooted; "Napoleon of India" (V.A. Smith); kaviraja, veena coins; ashvamedha; Meghavarman of Sri Lanka — Bodh Gaya monastery) → Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375–415; Shaka conquest — Gujarat/Malwa (Ujjain second capital); Mehrauli iron pillar ("Chandra"); Fa-hien; Navratnas — Kalidasa, Amarasimha, Varahamihira(?), Dhanvantari; Udayagiri caves (Vidisha) — Varaha) → Kumaragupta I (Nalanda founded; Huna threat; Mahendraditya) → Skandagupta (Huna repulse; Junagadh inscription — Sudarshana repaired again; Bhitari pillar) → decline (Hunas — Toramana, Mihirakula; feudatories; Yashodharman — Mandasor 532).
  • Administration: bhukti (uparika) → vishaya (vishayapati; adhikarana board — nagarasreshthi, sarthavaha, prathama-kulika, prathama-kayastha) → vithi → grama; land grants (agrahara, brahmadeya) → feudalism debate; taxes udranga, uparikara, bhaga, bhoga, vishti (forced labour); dinara (gold), rupaka (silver), fewer copper coins; guilds (shreni; Mandasor silk-weavers); Kumaramatyas, sandhivigrahika.
  • Culture: Sanskrit peak — Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava, Ritusamhara, Malavikagnimitram, Vikramorvashiyam), Shudraka Mrichchhakatika, Vishakhadatta Mudrarakshasa & Devichandraguptam, Amarasimha Amarakosha, Vishnu Sharma Panchatantra; Puranas finalised; Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya 499; zero-place value, π, rotation, eclipses), Varahamihira (Brihat Samhita, Pancha-siddhantika), Brahmagupta (628 — later), Vagbhata; Nalanda; Dashavatara temple Deogarh, Bhitargaon brick temple, Sanchi Temple 17, Ajanta caves 16, 17, 19 (Vakataka Harishena), Bagh caves, Sarnath Buddha (sandstone), Sultanganj copper Buddha; Vishnu-Bhagavata cult; iron pillar rustless; Nagara style origins; shikhara appears.
  • Fa-hien (399–414): peaceful, Chandalas outside towns, no capital punishment, Pataliputra hospital.

Traps

  • Junagadh inscription = Rudradaman (Sanskrit, 150 CE) and also Skandagupta's record — same rock, both mention Sudarshana lake.
  • Allahabad prashasti = Harishena (Samudragupta), on Ashoka's pillar; Mehrauli pillar = Chandragupta II.
  • Nalanda was founded by Kumaragupta I, patronised later by Harsha and the Palas.
  • Shaka era 78 CE = Kanishka's accession (used in India's national calendar).

Pair-recall sheet.

Pairs flash

  • Milindapanha → Menander × Nagasena · Heliodorus pillar → Besnagar.
  • Junagadh (Sudarshana) → Rudradaman · St. Thomas → Gondophernes.
  • Saka era → 78 CE Kanishka · council → 4th, Kundalvana · capitals → Purushpura + Mathura.
  • Gautamiputra's eulogist → mother Gautami Balashri (Nasik) · Satavahana coins → lead.
  • Muziris → Chera pepper port · Puhar → Chola · pearl → Pandya.
  • Prayaga Prashasti → Harisena · Nalanda → Kumaragupta I · Fa-Hien → CG II.
  • Aryabhatiya → 499 · iron pillar → 'Chandra' · Deogarh → Dashavatara temple.
  • Kalidasa court → CG II · Banabhatta → Harsha (Harshacharita) · Xuanzang → Nalanda + Kannauj assembly.
  • Land grants first regular → Satavahanas/Guptas (agrahara) · kumaramatya → Gupta officer.
  • Silk Road empire → Kushana · Buddha image first → Gandhara & Mathura.

Trap flash

  • Samudragupta's pillar inscription is on Ashoka's Allahabad pillar (added later — don't confuse authors).
  • Gupta 'golden age' critique: women/shudra position, urban trade dip — quote-ready nuance.
  • Saka era (78) ≠ Vikram Samvat (57 BCE) ≠ Gupta era (320).
  • Ajanta caves = Gupta-Vakataka mix; Ellora-Kailasa = Rashtrakuta (later).

Previous Year Questions

What the examiner has actually asked.

10 original prelims-pattern questions; key with one-line reasoning at the end.

Q1. The Junagadh rock inscription of 150 CE, the first long Sanskrit inscription, belongs to: (a) Gautamiputra Satakarni (b) Rudradaman I (c) Kanishka (d) Samudragupta

Q2. The Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar records the devotion of a Greek ambassador to: (a) Buddha (b) Shiva (c) Vasudeva (d) Surya

Q3. Match: A. Gandhara — 1. red sandstone · B. Mathura — 2. white marble · C. Amaravati — 3. grey schist (a) A-3 B-1 C-2 (b) A-1 B-3 C-2 (c) A-2 B-1 C-3 (d) A-3 B-2 C-1

Q4. Consider the Satavahanas: 1. They issued coins mainly in lead. 2. They used matronymics. 3. Naneghat inscription records the earliest land grant to Brahmanas. (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 and 3 (c) 1 and 3 (d) 1, 2 and 3

Q5. The Allahabad pillar inscription was composed by: (a) Harishena (b) Ravikirti (c) Banabhatta (d) Vasumitra

Q6. Which Gupta ruler is credited with founding Nalanda Mahavihara? (a) Chandragupta I (b) Samudragupta (c) Kumaragupta I (d) Skandagupta

Q7. The Gupta district-level administrative board (adhikarana) included: 1. Nagarasreshthi 2. Sarthavaha 3. Prathama-kulika 4. Sandhivigrahika (a) 1, 2 and 3 (b) 1 and 4 (c) 2, 3 and 4 (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Q8. Vishti in Gupta records refers to: (a) Land tax (b) Forced labour (c) Gold coin (d) Royal grant

Q9. The Shaka era (78 CE), used in India's national calendar, is associated with: (a) Rudradaman (b) Kanishka (c) Nahapana (d) Menander

Q10. Ajanta caves 16, 17 and 19 were excavated under the patronage of the: (a) Satavahanas (b) Vakatakas (c) Chalukyas (d) Rashtrakutas

Answer key

QAnsWhy
1bWestern Kshatrapa; Sudarshana lake repair.
2cGaruda pillar of the Bhagavata cult, c. 113 BCE.
3aStandard material triad.
4dAll correct.
5aHarishena, Samudragupta's sandhivigrahika.
6cKumaragupta I (Shakraditya per Xuanzang).
7aSandhivigrahika was the minister of peace and war at court.
8bForced labour, also in Maurya-era texts.
9bKanishka's accession, 78 CE.
10bVakataka minister Varahadeva under Harishena, 5th c.

Part I — GS Paper I — General Studies (Prelims) · Chapter 1: History & Indian Culture

Lesson 1.1.15

Architecture: Temple Styles, Forts & Monuments

In this lessonDetailed StudyRevision DigestKey Points & MindmapDiagrams, Maps & FlowchartsPrevious Year Questions

Detailed Study

The full treatment of this lesson.

Four exam arenas: stupas & caves, temple styles, Indo-Islamic, modern-colonial. Every question is a match-the-pair.

1. Stupas & caves

  • Stupa anatomy: anda (dome) on medhi, harmika railing-box, chhatra umbrellas, vedika railing, torana gates (Sanchi's four — Satavahana-era carvings: Jatakas, aniconic Buddha).
  • Sequence: Ashoka core (Sanchi-1, Bharhut, Piprahwa relic-claims) → Sunga railings → Satavahana gates (Sanchi) → Amaravati (white-marble narrative, Satavahana-Ikshvaku) → Gandhara dharmarajika (Kanishka's relic chambers).
  • Caves: Barabar (Ashoka, Lomas Rishi chaitya-arch facade — earliest) → western chaitya-vihara schools (Bhaja, Kondane, Karle — Karle chaitya grandest, Nashik Pandav leni inscriptions of Gautamiputra/Ushavadata) → Ajanta (Hinayana + Mahayana phases: 9,10,12,13 early; 1,2,16,17 Vakataka) → Ellora (Buddhist-Hindu-Jain; Kailasa temple 16 — Rashtrakuta Krishna I, monolithic) → Elephanta (Shiva panels — Rashtrakuta attribution) → Jain rows (Gwalior, Ellora 30-34).

2. Temple styles

StyleSignatureAnchors
NagaraCurvilinear shikhara, amalaka-kalasha, panchayatanaKhajuraho Kandariya (Chandelas); Odisha: Lingaraja, Konark Sun-wheel (Ganga Narasimhadeva I); Solanki Modhera; Masrur monolith
DravidaPyramidal vimana, gopuram, mandapasPallava rathas + Shore (Narasimhavarman I/II, Mamalla/Mamallapuram); Chola Brihadeshwara (Rajaraja I, 1010) + Gangaikondacholapuram; Pandya gopurams; Vijayanagara-Nayaka additions (Madurai)
VesaraHybrid; star-plans (Hoysala)Chalukya Badami + Pattadakal (UNESCO — both styles side-by-side); Rashtrakuta Kailasa; Hoysaleswara Halebidu, Chennakesava Belur, Keshava Somnathpur

3. Indo-Islamic arc

  • Sultanate: Qutub Minar (Iltutmish completes; Aibak begins), Alai Darwaza (Alauddin — first true arch + dome finishing), Tughlaq battered walls + sloping, Khirki mosque (Khan-i-Jahan), Lodi octagonal tomb-gardens (first garden tombs), Jaunpur Sharqui, Bengal curved-roof (Adina mosque, Pandua), Gujarat white-marble blends.
  • Mughal: Humayun's tomb (first grand garden tomb, charbagh), Purana Qila, Akbar: Fatehpur Sikri (Buland Darwaza; Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas pillar; red sandstone + Gujarati-Chaulukya brackets), Allahabad/Agra forts, Shah Jahan: Taj (1632-53; pietra dura, double dome), Jama Masjid, Red Fort (Diwan-i-Am/Khas, Rang Mahal), Shalimar (Lahore); Sikh: Harmandir Sahib (gold leaf — Ranjit Singh era); Rajput: Amber, Mehrangarh, Udaipur palaces.
  • Colonial: classical revival (Victoria Memorial — Indo-Saracenic hybrid is different: Chepauk, Gateway of India, Lutyens' New Delhi blend — Viceroy's House dome).

MCQ hooks

  • First true arch/dome → Alai Darwaza; first garden tomb → Humayun's; charbagh peak → Taj.
  • Pietra dura (parchin kari) = Taj inlay; panch mahal = Fatehpur Sikri.
  • Kailasa (Ellora 16) carved top-down monolith = Krishna I.
  • Stupa 'anda-harmika-chhatra' order asked verbatim.
  • Konark wheels = sundial function; jagamohana type = deul pair (Odisha: rekha deul + pidha deul).
  • Hoysala star platform + soapstone = Vesara terminal glory.

Temple styles (Shilpa texts: Nagara north, Dravida south, Vesara Deccan)

FeatureNagaraDravidaVesara
Superstructureshikhara curvilinear (rekha-prasada); amalaka + kalasha on topvimana pyramidal storeys (talas); stupi/shikhara octagonal caphybrid; shorter vimana
Enclosureusually nonehigh walls, gopuram gateways, tank—

Sub-schoolsOdisha/Kalinga (deul, jagamohana, rekha/pidha/khakhara deul; Lingaraja, Konark, Jagannath, Mukteshwar), Khajuraho/Chandela (Kandariya Mahadeva; sandstone; erotic panels; high jagati), Solanki/Maru-Gurjara (Modhera Sun; Dilwara — marble), latina, phamsana, valabhi shikhara typesPallava (rock-cut Mahabalipuram rathas, Shore temple; structural Kanchi Kailasanatha), Chola (Brihadishvara 1010 — 66 m vimana, monolithic 80-ton shikhara), Pandya (gopuram emphasis), Vijayanagara (kalyana mandapa, raya gopuram, Vitthala), Nayaka (Madurai Meenakshi — prakaras, 1000-pillar hall)Chalukya (Badami rock-cut; Aihole — Durga (apsidal), Ladkhan; Pattadakal — Virupaksha (Dravida), Papanatha (Nagara)), Rashtrakuta (Kailasa Ellora), Hoysala (Belur Chennakeshava, Halebidu Hoysaleshwara, Somnathpur; soapstone; stellate; UNESCO 2023)
  • Others: Kashmir (Martand Sun — Lalitaditya; trefoil arches, pyramidal roofs), Bengal (chala & ratna terracotta — Bishnupur), Kerala (sloping roofs, circular sreekovil), Himachal (pagoda — Hidimba).
  • Cave & stupa: Barabar (Maurya) → Bhaja, Karle, Kanheri (chaitya with wooden ribs; vihara) → Ajanta (1–29; 9 & 10 Satavahana chaityas; 16, 17, 19 Vakataka; murals), Ellora (34: 1–12 Buddhist, 13–29 Hindu, 30–34 Jain; Kailasa cave 16), Elephanta (Trimurti), Udayagiri-Khandagiri (Jain, Kharavela), Bagh, Badami. Stupa parts: anda, harmika, yashti, chhatra, medhi, vedika, torana, pradakshina patha; Sanchi (Ashoka; Shunga railing; Satavahana gateways), Bharhut, Amaravati, Dhamek (Sarnath, Gupta), Piprahwa, Kesariya (largest), Kanaganahalli.

Indo-Islamic (arch, dome, minaret, pietra dura, jali, charbagh)

  • Sultanate: Qutb complex (Aibak-Iltutmish; Alai Darwaza 1311), Tughlaq batter (Tughlaqabad, Firoz Shah Kotla), Lodi octagonal tombs & double dome (Lodi Gardens, Sikandar Lodi).
  • Provincial: Bengal (Adina mosque Pandua; bangla roof), Jaunpur (Atala — propylon screens), Gujarat (Jama Masjid Ahmedabad; Sidi Saiyyed jali; Sarkhej), Malwa (Mandu — Jahaz Mahal, Hindola Mahal), Bijapur (Gol Gumbaz — 2nd largest dome; Ibrahim Rauza), Golconda (Charminar 1591), Bidar (Gawan madrasa).
  • Mughal: Humayun's tomb (charbagh prototype), Fatehpur Sikri (red sandstone; Buland Darwaza; Salim Chishti tomb marble), Agra fort, Akbar's tomb Sikandra, Itimad-ud-Daula (pietra dura), Taj Mahal (Ustad Ahmad Lahauri; 1632–53), Red Fort & Jama Masjid Delhi, Badshahi Lahore, Bibi ka Maqbara (1660s).
  • Sikh: Harmandir Sahib 1589–1604 (Guru Arjan; gold Ranjit Singh 1830). Rajput: Chittor (Kirti Stambh Jain 12th c., Vijay Stambh 1448 Rana Kumbha), Kumbhalgarh (36-km wall), Amber, Mehrangarh, Jaisalmer, Hawa Mahal 1799 (Pratap Singh; Lal Chand Ustad), Jantar Mantar (Jai Singh II; 5 — Delhi, Jaipur (UNESCO), Ujjain, Varanasi, Mathura lost). Stepwells: Rani ki Vav (11th c., UNESCO 2014), Chand Baori (Abhaneri, 9th c.), Adalaj (1499).

Colonial

  • Indo-Saracenic (Chepauk, Victoria Memorial (Emerson), Gateway of India (Wittet, 1924), Madras High Court, Mysore Palace (Irwin)), Gothic revival (CST Mumbai — Stevens, UNESCO 2004; Bombay University), neoclassical (Raj Bhavan Kolkata, Town Hall Mumbai), New Delhi (Lutyens — Rashtrapati Bhavan (Sanchi-style dome); Baker — Secretariats, Parliament House 1927), Art Deco Marine Drive (UNESCO 2018), Portuguese Goa churches (Bom Jesus — Xavier relics; Se Cathedral), French Pondicherry.

UNESCO recent (India total 43 as of 2024)

  • 2021 Dholavira & Ramappa (Kakatiya Rudreshwara) · 2023 Santiniketan & Hoysala ensembles · 2024 Moidams (Charaideo, Ahom) · Tentative list items keep appearing in news (Maratha Military Landscapes — inscribed 2025).

Traps

  • Gopuram dominance grows later (Pandya/Nayaka), not in early Pallava temples.
  • Konark is a Sun temple of the Eastern Gangas (Narasimhadeva I) — not Chola.
  • Gol Gumbaz is Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Charminar Golconda (Qutb Shahi).
  • Hoysala temples use soapstone (chloritic schist); Khajuraho sandstone; Dilwara marble.

Key Points & Mindmap

Skeleton facts and recall triggers.

Match-pair drills.

Pairs flash

  • Lomas Rishi chaitya-arch → Barabar (Ashoka) · grandest chaitya → Karle.
  • Sanchi toranas → Satavahana carvings · Amaravati → white marble narrative.
  • Kailasa Ellora → Krishna I (Rashtrakuta), top-down · Elephanta Shiva → Rashtrakuta line.
  • Kandariya → Chandelas · Konark → Eastern Gangas · Modhera → Solankis.
  • Brihadeshwara → Rajaraja I 1010 · Gangaikondacholapuram → Rajendra I.
  • Pattadakal → Chalukya (UNESCO) · Belur-Halebidu → Hoysala star plans.
  • Alai Darwaza → first true arch+gate dome · sloping walls → Tughlaqs.
  • First garden tomb → Humayun's · Buland Darwaza → Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar).
  • Pietra dura → Taj · Panch Mahal → Fatehpur Sikri · Peacock throne → Shah Jahan.
  • Adina mosque → Bengal Pandua · curved roofs → Bengal style · Victoria Memorial → Indo-Saracenic.

Style-order flash

  • Stupa anatomy: medhi → anda → harmika → chhatra; gates = torana, railing = vedika.
  • Nagara = shikhara/amalaka; Dravida = vimana/gopuram; Vesara = hybrid/star.
  • Odisha temple pair: rekha deul (sanctum) + pidha deul (hall).

Trap flash

  • Qutub Minar begun by Aibak, finished by Iltutmish (Firoz repaired top).
  • Shore Temple = Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha), not Mamalla I.
  • Ajanta ≠ Ellora: Ajanta = Buddhist only; Ellora = tri-faith.
  • First true arch in Sultanate masonry = Alai Darwaza (Alauddin).

Previous Year Questions

8 original prelims-pattern questions; key with one-line reasoning at the end.

Q1. Which of the following is a feature of the Nagara style rather than Dravida? (a) Enclosure walls with gopurams (b) Curvilinear shikhara topped by an amalaka (c) Storeyed pyramidal vimana (d) A temple tank within the complex

Q2. Consider the Hoysala temples: 1. Built mainly of soapstone. 2. Have stellate (star-shaped) plans. 3. Belur and Halebidu were inscribed as UNESCO sites in 2023. (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 and 3 (c) 1 and 3 (d) 1, 2 and 3

Q3. Match: A. Rekha deul — 1. Khajuraho · B. Panchayatana on high jagati — 2. Odisha · C. Trefoil arches — 3. Kashmir (a) A-2 B-1 C-3 (b) A-1 B-2 C-3 (c) A-3 B-1 C-2 (d) A-2 B-3 C-1

Part I — GS Paper I — General Studies (Prelims) · Chapter 1: History & Indian Culture

Lesson 1.1.16

Painting: Miniature, Mughal & Modern Schools

In this lessonDetailed StudyRevision DigestKey Points & MindmapDiagrams, Maps & FlowchartsPrevious Year Questions

Detailed Study

The full treatment of this lesson.

Chain: wall murals → palm-leaf minis → Mughal atelier → Rajasthani-Pahari offshoots → folk living traditions. Pair school-patron-signature.

1. Wall murals

  • Ajanta (2nd BCE–6th CE): tempera (fresco-secco) on mud-plaster; icons: Padmapani (cave 1), Dying Princess (16), Bodhisattva & Jataka panels (17); Chalukya Badami, Pallava Panamalai panels; Kailasa (Ellora) Shaiva panels; Lepakshi (Vijayanagara, Veerabhadra — hanging pillar lore); Kerala: Mattancherry (Ramayana panels), Guruvayur; Odisha: Raghurajpur pata-chitra (palm + cloth).
  • Technique note: true fresco (wet lime) vs Indian tempera (dry plaster + binder) — one-line differentiator.

2. Miniature arc

  • Pala (Bengal-Bihar, 8th-12th): palm-leaf Buddhist manuscripts, monastic patronage, Vajrayana icons.
  • Jain (western Indian): Kalpasutra/Kalakacharya katha; Gujarat-Rajasthan; profuse gold, 'pata' style; profile eyes convention; paper from 13th-14th c.
  • Mughal: Humayun returns from Persia with Mir Sayyid Ali + Abdus Samad → the imperial atelier is born; Akbar: Tutinama, Hamzanama (1400 folios), Razmnama (Mahabharata Persian), Akbarnama — Indian-Persian synthesis, Daswant and Basawan masters; Jahangir: connoisseur peak — portraits, flora-fauna (Ustad Mansur — dodo/painted stork), European prints arrive (Jesuit missions); Shah Jahan: courtly polish, jewel tones, formal borders, harem albums, Padshahnama; decline post-aurangzeb → provincial offshoots (Awadh, Murshidabad).
  • Rajasthani (Rajput courts): Mewar (Chawand Ragamala 1605, Mewar Ramayana), Kishangarh (Bani-Thani — Savant Singh-Nihal Chand), Bundi-Kota (hunting, love scenes), Bikaner (Mughal-trained), Jodhpur (Marwar bold), Dhundhar-Amber-Jaipur; themes: Ragamala, Baramasa, Bhagavata, Gita-Govinda.
  • Pahari (Himalayan foothills): Basohli (c.1660-90 — bold primaries, Rasamanjari (Devidasa atelier); 'Chaurapanchasika' lineage), Kangra (post-1765 Guler-trained: Manaku-Nainsukh family; Gita-Govinda, Bihari Satsai; lyric wash style under Raja Sansar Chand), Guler (first naturalism), Garhwal, Jammu.
  • Deccan: Bijapur (Ibrahim Adil Shah II), Golconda (lush gold, dancing girls), Ahmadnagar ('Nujum al-Ulum' manuscript).

3. Folk-tribal living traditions

  • Madhubani/Mithila (Bihar): kohbar (wedding-chamber) symbols; fish motif; women-led; Bharni-Kachni styles; post-1934 earthquake revival credit (William Archer documentation).
  • Warli (Maharashtra): white rice-paste on mud walls, tarpa dance circles, chauk (marriage square), Jivya Soma Mashe revival.
  • Phad (Shahpura, Rajasthan): Pabuji-Devnarayan epic scrolls, bhopa-bhopi performance.
  • Patachitra: Odisha (Jagannath icons) + Bengal (Patua scroll-singers), Sanjhi (Mathura paper-stencil).
  • Kalamkari (Andhra-Telangana): Srikalahasti (pen) vs Machilipatnam (block) — draw-with-pen vs block-print; myrobalan + mordant chemistry.
  • Gond (MP), Pithora (Gujarat-Rajasthan, Bhilala), Cheriyal (Telangana scrolls), Thangka (Ladakh-Sikkim-Tawang — Vajrayana iconometry), Manjusha (Bihar), Kalighat (Bengal pat).

MCQ hooks

  • Bani-Thani = Kishangarh; 'India's Mona Lisa' tag.
  • Mansur = Jahangir's animal painter; Hamzanama = Akbar launch project.
  • Basohli vs Kangra: bold vs lyrical; Nainsukh = Guler-trained realist.
  • Kalamkari twin towns: Srikalahasti pen, Machilipatnam block.
  • Warli tarpa circle ≠ Madhubani kohbar.
  • Ajanta tempera ≠ European true fresco.

Revision Digest

Condensed for the last mile before the exam.

Prelims GS-I › History & Culture › Art & Culture. School-identification by patron/theme/palette; a favourite for "consider the following" questions.

Pre-historic & cave

  • Bhimbetka (MP; Wakankar 1957; Mesolithic hunting scenes; UNESCO 2003).
  • Ajanta (2nd BCE–6th CE; tempera/fresco-secco on dry plaster; Padmapani & Vajrapani (cave 1), Dying Princess (16), Jataka narratives; Vakataka phase), Bagh (MP; Gupta; secular), Sittanavasal (TN; Pandya; Jain; lotus pond), Ellora (Kailasa ceiling), Badami (Chalukya Mangalesha, cave 3 — earliest Brahmanical), Lepakshi (Vijayanagara; Veerabhadra; no primary colours, black outlines), Armamalai, Jogimara (Chhattisgarh; earliest c. 1st BCE), Kerala murals (Mattancherry, Padmanabhapuram).
  • Vishnudharmottara Purana (Chitrasutra; shadanga — six limbs of painting, cited via Vatsyayana).

Manuscript/miniature (east & west)

  • Pala (9th–12th; palm-leaf; Buddhist — Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita; Dhiman & Vitpala; sinuous lines) → Western Indian/Apabhramsa (Gujarat-Rajasthan; Jain Kalpasutra, Kalakacharya Katha; protruding farther eye, angular faces; 11th–15th c.).
  • Sultanate/pre-Mughal: Nimatnama (Mandu, c. 1500), Chaurapanchasika group, Laur-Chanda.

Mughal school

  • Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali & Abdus Samad (Persian Safavid). Akbar: Tutinama, Hamzanama (1,400 large cloth folios), Razmnama, Akbarnama; artists Daswant, Basawan, Miskin, Kesu Das; tasvir khana; European influence (Jesuits, 1580). Jahangir: peak — naturalism, portraiture, Ustad Mansur (birds/animals — Nadir-ul-Asr; Siberian crane, dodo, zebra), Abul Hasan (Nadir-uz-Zaman), Bishandas, Manohar; allegorical Jahangir preferring a Sufi sheikh; muraqqa albums; halo. Shah Jahan: formal, court scenes, Padshahnama, margins; Aurangzeb: decline; artists migrate → provincial/Rajput/Pahari.
  • Deccani: Ahmednagar (Tarif-i-Husain Shahi), Bijapur (Ibrahim Adil Shah II — Nujum-ul-Ulum; Ragamala), Golconda; Persian + Turkish + Vijayanagara elements; lavish gold, tall figures; Hyderabad later.

Rajasthani (Rajput) schools

  • Mewar (Sahibdin — Ragamala 1605 Chawand; Rasikapriya; Nathdwara pichhwai — Shrinathji), Marwar/Jodhpur (Pabuji ki phad; Man Singh), Bikaner (Mughal-influenced; Usta family), Bundi (lush landscapes, Ragamala, Chitrashala), Kota (hunting scenes), Kishangarh (**Nihal Chand — Bani Thani, Savant Singh; elongated eyes), Jaipur/Amber** (Sahib Ram; large portraits), Malwa (bold flat colours), Alwar.

Pahari schools

  • Basohli (earliest, 17th c.; bold primary colours, beetle-wing cases for jewels, Rasamanjari of Devidasa 1694), Guler (Nainsukh, Manaku — Pandit Seu family; soft, lyrical), Kangra (Sansar Chand; Gita Govinda, Bhagavata, Nala-Damayanti; delicate feminine ideal), Chamba (rumal embroidery too), Garhwal (Mola Ram), Kulu, Mandi, Jammu.

Company & Modern

  • Company school (Patna/Kalighat/Delhi/Tanjore-Trichy; Sewak Ram, Ghulam Ali Khan; watercolour for British patrons), Kalighat pats (19th c.; bold brush; satire), Tanjore/Mysore (gesso, gold leaf, glass; Maratha & Wodeyar patronage).
  • Raja Ravi Varma (Kerala; oil, academic realism; oleograph press Lonavala 1894; Shakuntala, Damayanti), Bengal school (Abanindranath — Bharat Mata 1905, wash technique; E.B. Havell; Nandalal Bose — Haripura posters, Constitution illustrations; Asit Haldar, Kshitindranath Majumdar), Amrita Sher-Gil (Three Girls, Bride's Toilet), Jamini Roy (Kalighat folk revival), Rabindranath (doodles), Gaganendranath (cubism), Progressive Artists' Group 1947 (Souza, Raza, Husain, Ara, Bakre, Gade), K.G. Subramanyan, Tyeb Mehta, Bhupen Khakhar, Ram Kinker Baij (sculptor, Santhal Family).

Folk & tribal (GI-tagged mostly)

  • Madhubani/Mithila (Bihar; Kohbar; natural dyes; Sita Devi, Ganga Devi), Warli (Maharashtra; white on mud; Jivya Soma Mashe), Pattachitra (Odisha; Raghurajpur; Jagannath), Kalamkari (Srikalahasti pen; Machilipatnam block), Gond (MP; Jangarh Singh Shyam; dots/dashes), Pithora (Rathwa, Gujarat), Phad (Rajasthan scroll), Cheriyal scrolls (Telangana), Thangka (Buddhist), Saura (Odisha), Rogan (Kutch; castor oil), Kalighat, Mata ni Pachedi (Gujarat), Sohrai & Khovar (Jharkhand; GI 2020), Manjusha (Bihar), Kavad (Rajasthan), Chitrakathi (Maharashtra), Tholu Bommalata (AP leather puppets), Mandana, Aipan (Uttarakhand), Chittara (Karnataka), Pichhwai.

Traps

  • Ajanta is tempera, not true fresco; Padmapani is cave 1.
  • Bani Thani = Kishangarh (Nihal Chand); Bharat Mata = Abanindranath; Haripura posters = Nandalal.
  • Basohli is the earliest Pahari school; Kangra the most refined.

Key Points & Mindmap

Skeleton facts and recall triggers.

School → patron → signature drills.

Pairs flash

  • Padmapani/Dying Princess → Ajanta (tempera) · Lepakshi → Vijayanagara murals · Mattancherry → Kerala.
  • Pala → palm-leaf Buddhist · Jain school → Kalpasutra, Gujarat gold.
  • Hamzanama/Tutinama/Razmnama → Akbar · Mansur flora-fauna → Jahangir · Padshahnama polish → Shah Jahan.
  • Mir Sayyid Ali + Abdus Samad → arrive under Humayun · Bichitr/Bishandas → Jahangir portraits embassy scene.
  • Chawand Ragamala → Mewar 1605 · Bani-Thani → Kishangarh (Nihal Chand) · Rasamanjari → Basohli · Gita-Govinda lyrical → Kangra.
  • Manaku-Nainsukh → Guler-Kangra family · Sansar Chand → Kangra patron raja.
  • Srikalahasti → pen kalamkari · Machilipatnam → block kalamkari.
  • Kohbar → Madhubani · tarpa + chauk → Warli · Pabuji scroll → Phad · Jagannath → Odisha pata.
  • Thangka → Ladakh/Sikkim · Cheriyal → Telangana · Sanjhi stencil → Mathura.
  • Golconda-Bijapur → Deccan lush miniatures · Nujum al-Ulum → Ahmadnagar.

Trap flash

  • Kangra ≠ Basohli (lyrical vs bold); both = Pahari.
  • Mughal art declines under Aurangzeb (patron cut) — not a new school.
  • Bani-Thani painter = Nihal Chand, patron-poet = Savant Singh.
  • Madhubani revival credit → 1934 earthquake + Archer surveys, not post-Independence only.
  • Razmnama = Persian Mahabharata (Akbar), NOT Ramayana (that = Ramayana translations under Akbar too).

Part I — GS Paper I — General Studies (Prelims) · Chapter 1: History & Indian Culture

Lesson 1.1.17

Music, Dance & Theatre Forms

In this lessonDetailed StudyRevision DigestKey Points & MindmapDiagrams, Maps & FlowchartsPrevious Year Questions

Detailed Study

The full treatment of this lesson.

Two lists to memorise: 8 classical dances and the two music systems' anchors, plus folk favourites.

1. The 8 classical dances (Sangeet Natak Akademi)

DanceStateSignatures
BharatanatyamTamil NaduSolo temple (agamic) art; adavus (units), abhinaya (expression); repertory: alarippu→jatiswaram→varnam→tillana; nattuvanar conducts; devadasi ('sadhir') lineage; Rukmini Devi revival (Kalakshetra 1936)
KathakUP/NorthStorytelling 'katha'; gharanas: Lucknow (grace, Wajid Ali Shah era), Jaipur (virtuoso footwork), Benares; chakkars, tatkar; nritta+nritya; Mughal court phase
KathakaliKerala'Story-play'; all-male tradition; vesham colour codes (pacha green = noble, red beard = evil); mudra lexicon; chenda-maddalam; Krishnanattam-Ramanattam lineage
KuchipudiAndhraVillage Kuchelapuram; Brahmin-bhagavathulu troupe plays; tarangam (plate dance on brass); Bhama Kalapam (Siddhendra Yogi)
OdissiOdishatribhanga S-bend; temple Maharis → gotipua boy-troupes; texts: Gitagovinda, Abhinaya Chandrika; chauka & tribhanga basics
ManipuriManipurRas Leela (Bhagyachandra codified); pung cholom drum dance; soft knee-curve; Lai Haraoba roots
MohiniyattamKerala'Enchantress'; lasya-dominant; white-gold costume, left-side hair bun; Swati Tirunal compositions; Vallathol revival (Kerala Kalamandalam 1930)
SattriyaAssamSankaradeva's Vaishnavite sattras; ankiya naat plays; gayan-bayan musicians; monastic and naturalistic streams

2. Music systems

  • Sangeet trinity (Natyashastra): vocal (geet), instrumental (vadya), dance (nritya). Rasa theory: 8 rasas + shanta (9th).
  • Hindustani (north): gharana system; dhrupad (oldest gravitas), khayal (Amir Khusrau attribution; Sadarang popularised), thumri (semi-classical), tarana; instruments: sitar (Khusrau lineage claim), sarod, sarangi, tabla, shehnai (Bismillah Khan), santoor (Shivkumar Sharma); Tansen (Akbar's Navaratna — Miyan ki malhar).
  • Carnatic (south): kritis; Trinity — Tyagaraja, Muttuswami Dikshitar, Syama Sastri; structure: pallavi-anupallavi-charanam; 72 melakarta scheme (Venkatamakhin's Chaturdandi Prakasika line); instruments: veena, mridangam, ghatam, kanjira, violin (adapted — Baluswami Dikshitar credit line), nadaswaram.

3. Folk & theatre anchors

  • Yakshagana (Karnataka), Theyyam (Kerala possession-ritual), Bhavai (Gujarat), Tamasha (MH — Lavani), Nautanki (UP), Jatra (Bengal), Bhand Pather (Kashmir), Kutiyattam (Sanskrit drama, UNESCO).
  • Folk dances: Bhangra/Giddha (Punjab), Garba-Dandiya (Gujarat), Lavani (MH), Ghoomar/Kalbelia (Rajasthan — Kalbelia UNESCO), Bihu (Assam), Chhau (Jharkhand-Odisha-WB masks — UNESCO), Rouf (Kashmir), Dalkhai (Odisha), Koli (Maharashtra coast), Dumhal (Kashmir).

MCQ hooks

  • Natyashastra = Bharata (600-200 BCE span); 'dasarupaka' = Dhananjaya (10 forms).
  • Sattriya = newest to classical list (2000); 8-list order often asked.
  • Kathak gharana city mismatch = classic trap (Jaipur gharana ≠ Lucknow grace).
  • Carnatic Trinity order Tyagaraja-Dikshitar-Syama Sastri; Hindustani counterpart = 'Tansen line'.
  • Pung cholom = Manipur; Chenda = Kathakali; Mizhavu = Kutiyattam.
  • Kalakshetra = Rukmini Devi (1936); Kalamandalam = Vallathol (1930).

Prelims GS-I › History & Culture › Art & Culture. State–form–exponent matching plus instrument classification.

Classical dance (8 recognised by Sangeet Natak Akademi; Ministry lists 8 — Chhau is SNA-listed too)

(Chhau)Seraikela (Jharkhand), Mayurbhanj (Odisha), Purulia (WB)martial, masks (except Mayurbhanj)UNESCO 2010
  • Natya Shastra (Bharata, c. 200 BCE–200 CE): rasa (8 + shanta by Abhinavagupta), bhava, tandava/lasya, nritta/nritya/natya, four abhinaya (angika, vachika, aharya, sattvika), karanas 108.

Classical music

  • Hindustani: dhrupad (Gwalior; Tansen, Dagar; alap-jod-jhala, pakhawaj; Man Singh Tomar), khayal (Sadarang/Niyamat Khan, Muhammad Shah Rangila), thumri (Lucknow; Wajid Ali Shah), tappa (Punjab camel-drivers; Shori Miyan), tarana (Khusrau attribution), ghazal, qawwali (Khusrau); gharanas — Gwalior (oldest), Agra, Kirana (Abdul Karim Khan; Bhimsen Joshi), Jaipur-Atrauli (Alladiya; Kishori Amonkar), Patiala (Bade Ghulam Ali), Rampur-Sahaswan, Mewati (Jasraj), Benares (thumri; Girija Devi); raga (thaat 10 — Bhatkhande; vadi/samvadi; time theory), tala (teental 16, jhaptal 10, ektal 12, rupak 7, dadra 6, keherwa 8).
  • Carnatic: Trinity — Tyagaraja (Tiruvaiyaru; Telugu; Pancharatna kritis), Muthuswami Dikshitar (Sanskrit; Navagraha), Syama Sastri (Kamakshi; swarajati); Purandara Dasa (Pitamaha; Mayamalavagowla); Melakarta 72 (Venkatamakhin Chaturdandi Prakashika), kriti, varnam, ragam-tanam-pallavi, tillana, javali, padam; Swathi Thirunal; M.S. Subbulakshmi (Bharat Ratna 1998), Semmangudi, Balamuralikrishna; instruments veena, mridangam, ghatam, kanjira, nadaswaram, tavil, morsing.
  • Instruments (Natya Shastra classes): tata (strings — sitar, sarod, veena, santoor, sarangi, violin), sushira (wind — bansuri, shehnai, nadaswaram), avanaddha (percussion — tabla, pakhawaj, mridangam, dhol), ghana (idiophones — manjira, ghatam, jal tarang). Exponents: Bismillah Khan (shehnai), Ravi Shankar (sitar), Ali Akbar Khan/Amjad Ali (sarod), Hariprasad Chaurasia (bansuri), Shivkumar Sharma (santoor), Zakir Hussain (tabla), Ram Narayan (sarangi), L. Subramaniam (violin), Vikku Vinayakram (ghatam), Rudra veena (Asad Ali Khan).
  • Folk/semi-classical tags in news: Baul (Bengal; UNESCO 2008), Sankirtana Manipur (UNESCO 2013), Ramman (Uttarakhand; 2009), Mudiyettu (Kerala; 2010), Kalbelia (Rajasthan; 2010), Kutiyattam (Kerala; 2008; oldest Sanskrit theatre), Ramlila (2008), Vedic chanting (2008), Nowruz, Yoga (2016), Kumbh Mela (2017), Durga Puja Kolkata (2021), Garba (2023) — India has 15 ICH elements.

Theatre & folk drama

  • Classical Sanskrit theatre: Bhasa (Svapnavasavadattam), Kalidasa, Shudraka, Bhavabhuti (Uttararamacharita), Vishakhadatta; Kutiyattam (Kerala, temple koothambalam).
  • Folk: Yakshagana (Karnataka), Bhavai (Gujarat), Tamasha (Maharashtra; lavani), Nautanki (UP), Swang (Haryana), Jatra (Bengal), Ankiya Naat/Bhaona (Assam), Therukoothu (TN), Bhand Pather (Kashmir), Maach (MP), Dashavatar (Konkan), Krishnattam (Guruvayur), Mudiyettu/Theyyam/Padayani (Kerala ritual), Burrakatha/Veedhi Natakam (AP), Powada (Maratha ballads), Alha (Bundelkhand), Pandavani (Chhattisgarh; Teejan Bai), Khyal (Rajasthan), Gambhira (Bengal), Karyala (HP), Bidesia (Bihar; Bhikhari Thakur).
  • Puppetry: string — Kathputli (Raj), Kundhei (Odisha), Gombeyatta (Karnataka), Bommalattam (TN); shadow — Tholu Bommalata (AP), Togalu Gombeyatta (Karnataka), Ravanachhaya (Odisha), Tholpavakoothu (Kerala), Chamadyache Bahulya (Maharashtra); rod — Putul Nautch (Bengal), Yampuri (Bihar); glove — Pavakoothu (Kerala), Kundhei Nach (Odisha).

Traps

  • Sattriya recognised 2000; Manipuri dancers wear no ankle bells; Kathakali is male-dominated; Mohiniyattam female solo.
  • Purandara Dasa = "Pitamaha" of Carnatic; Bhatkhande = Hindustani thaat system; Vishnu Digambar Paluskar — Gandharva Mahavidyalaya 1901.
  • Baul (2008) and Kalbelia (2010) are ICH; Chhau 2010; Garba 2023 — India has 15.

Dance flash

  • Tribhanga → Odissi · tarangam plate → Kuchipudi · pacha green → Kathakali.

  • Sattras → Sattriya (Sankaradeva) · lasya left-bun → Mohiniyattam · Kalakshetra → Bharatanatyam revival.

Music flash

  • Carnatic Trinity → Tyagaraja, Dikshitar, Syama Sastri · kriti structure → pallavi-anupallavi-charanam.
  • Khayal → Amir Khusrau (attribution) · dhrupad → oldest gravitas · thumri → semi-classical.
  • Tansen → Akbar court, Miyan ki malhar · Bismillah Khan → shehnai · Shivkumar Sharma → santoor.
  • Melakarta 72 → Carnatic raga scheme · rasa count → 8 (+shanta).
  • Mizhavu → Kutiyattam · nadaswaram → temple south · sarangi → Hindustani accompaniment.

Folk flash (state)

  • Bihu-Assam · Garba-Gujarat · Lavani & Tamasha-MH · Ghoomar, Kalbelia-Raj · Chhau-JO-WB · Yakshagana-Karnataka · Theyyam-Kerala · Bhavai-Gujarat · Nautanki-UP · Jatra-Bengal · Rouf-Kashmir.

Trap flash

  • Kathakali = Kerala (NOT Kathak = UP); Mohiniyattam = Kerala too (two classical from Kerala).
  • Sattriya: Assam, Vaishnavite — not Bihu (folk).
  • Odissi texts = Gitagovinda (Jayadeva), not Natyashastra.
